node.label: Philippe Ariès
node.date_label: Histoire des populations françaises et de leurs attitudes devant la vie (1948) · L’Enfant et la vie familiale sous l’Ancien Régime (1960) · Centuries of Childhood: Robert Baldick translation (1962) · L’Homme devant la mort (1977)
node.description: A historian of family, childhood and attitudes toward death whose work made familiar social arrangements appear historically variable. The childhood argument concerns the historical recognition of childhood; it is not equivalent to claiming that earlier parents never loved their children. Linda Pollock’s criticism questions evidential representativeness and generalization. Jean-Claude Chamboredon’s obituary places Ariès’s studies in dialogue with sociological questions about institutions and modernity, while explaining their politically and professionally unusual setting.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Histoire des populations françaises et de leurs attitudes devant la vie depuis le XVIIIe siècle (1948); L’Enfant et la vie familiale sous l’Ancien Régime (1960); Centuries of Childhood, translated by Robert Baldick (1962); L’Homme devant la mort (1977).
node.scope_note: Ariès’s complete books are unread here. Existing Pollock primary-excerpt qualifications are retained and Chamboredon is named as the substantive reader. No absence-of-parental-affection claim. French originals and Baldick’s translation remain distinct. The death-day discrepancy is kept in life research rather than resolved by assumption.

proposed_edges.relationship: Makes the historical concept of childhood a problem for family history, while prompting disputes over sources and generalization.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The formulation retains Pollock’s distinction between concept and affection and her source criticism (1983 excerpt pp. 1–10, especially 2 and 6–9). It neither endorses Ariès’s chronology nor reassigns later writers’ stronger claims to him.

proposed_edges.relationship: Historicizes familiar family institutions and social attitudes, opening comparative questions between modernity and earlier arrangements.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Attributed to Jean-Claude Chamboredon, 1985 pp. 150–151, on the work’s sociological questions and the family/death studies. This is a named reader’s substantive assessment, not a claim that Ariès belonged to a single sociological school.
